1. Two datasets have the same range. Explain how they could still look completely different, and which measure from §3.3–3.4 would catch the difference.

The range uses only the two extremes. One dataset can be tightly clustered with one value at each end (9, 11, 11, 11, 13) while the other is spread evenly (9, 10, 11, 12, 13); both have range 4. The interquartile range, built from the middle 50% of the data, catches the difference: by the type 7 rule the first dataset has Q1 = Q3 = 11 and IQR = 0, and the second has IQR = 12 − 10 = 2.

2. A child’s weight is “at the 10th percentile” on a growth chart. Explain what that means without using the word “percentile”.

Among children of the same age and sex in the reference population, 10% weigh less than this child and 90% weigh more. The child is on the light side of the reference, but not extremely so.

3. For six women’s haemoglobin values, 9.0, 10.5, 11.0, 11.5, 12.0 and 14.0 g/dL, find Q1 and Q3 by the type 7 rule, the IQR, the quartile deviation and the coefficient of quartile deviation.

n = 6, already sorted. Q1 position = 1 + 5 × 0.25 = 2.25 → 10.5 + 0.25 × (11.0 − 10.5) = 10.625 g/dL. Q3 position = 1 + 5 × 0.75 = 4.75 → 11.5 + 0.75 × (12.0 − 11.5) = 11.875 g/dL. IQR = 11.875 − 10.625 = 1.25 g/dL. QD = 1.25 ÷ 2 = 0.625 g/dL. Coefficient of QD = 1.25 ÷ (11.875 + 10.625) = 1.25 ÷ 22.5 = 0.056.

1. Explain why variance squares the deviations instead of averaging them directly, and name one property squared deviations have that absolute deviations lack.

Raw deviations from the mean always sum to zero (Σ(x − x̄) = 0), so their average is zero for every dataset and says nothing about spread. Squaring removes the signs. Unlike absolute values, squares split cleanly: Σ(x − c)² = Σ(x − x̄)² + n(x̄ − c)² for any c. This identity shows that the mean minimises the sum of squares, gives the proof that E[Σ(x − x̄)²] = (n − 1)σ², and is the start of the sums-of-squares partitions used in ANOVA and regression.

2. For the six haemoglobin values in Checkpoint 3.1 (9.0, 10.5, 11.0, 11.5, 12.0, 14.0 g/dL), compute the mean, the sum of squares, s² and s. Then compute SS ÷ n and say why it is not the usual estimate of σ².

Σx = 68.0; mean = 68.0 ÷ 6 = 11.33 g/dL. Σx² = 784.5; SS = Σx² − (Σx)² ÷ n = 784.5 − 4624 ÷ 6 = 784.5 − 770.67 = 13.83. (Directly: deviations −2.33, −0.83, −0.33, 0.17, 0.67, 2.67; squares 5.44, 0.69, 0.11, 0.03, 0.44, 7.11; total 13.83.) s² = 13.83 ÷ 5 = 2.77 (g/dL)²; s = √2.77 = 1.66 g/dL. SS ÷ n = 13.83 ÷ 6 = 2.31. Deviations are measured from x̄, the point that minimises squared distance, and on average over repeated samples E[SS] = (n − 1)σ². So SS ÷ n underestimates σ² on average by the factor (n − 1)/n = 5/6. Dividing by n − 1 removes that bias.

3. A student writes: “SD = 1.66 g/dL, so on average each woman’s haemoglobin differs from the mean by 1.66 g/dL.” Correct the sentence, using the mean deviation of the same data.

The average absolute distance from the mean is the mean deviation: (2.33 + 0.83 + 0.33 + 0.17 + 0.67 + 2.67) ÷ 6 = 7.0 ÷ 6 = 1.17 g/dL. A correct sentence: “The SD is 1.66 g/dL, the root-mean-square distance from the mean. It gives the two women farthest from the mean (9.0 and 14.0 g/dL) extra weight, so it exceeds the mean deviation of 1.17 g/dL.”

1. You want to compare how variable height is with how variable weight is in the same children. Why can’t you compare raw SDs, and what do you compare instead? Compute it for heights with mean 85 cm, SD 4 cm and weights with mean 11.8 kg, SD 1.75 kg.

The SDs are in different units (cm and kg) and on different scales, so their sizes cannot be compared. Compare coefficients of variation, which are unit-free. Height: CV = 4 ÷ 85 × 100 = 4.7%. Weight: CV = 1.75 ÷ 11.8 × 100 = 14.8%. Relative to its own mean, weight is about three times as variable as height.

2. Describe a right-skewed distribution of hospital length of stay, and state the usual order of mean, median and mode. In one ward the mean stay is 6 days, the median 5 days and the SD 4 days: compute Pearson’s coefficient of skewness and the mode implied by the empirical relation.

Most patients cluster at short stays, and a long tail stretches toward a few very long stays. For such a unimodal right-skewed curve the order is usually mode < median < mean: the mean is pulled toward the tail. This is a rule of thumb that can fail, especially for discrete data such as whole days. Pearson Sk = 3(mean − median) ÷ SD = 3 × (6 − 5) ÷ 4 = 0.75 (positive: right skew). Empirical mode ≈ 3 × median − 2 × mean = 15 − 12 = 3 days.

3. A colleague says a platykurtic distribution “must have a flat top”. Is that right? Explain what kurtosis actually measures.

No. Kurtosis, b₂ = m₄ ÷ m₂², is dominated by the fourth powers of the largest deviations, so it measures tail extremity: how prone the distribution is to extreme values relative to a Normal distribution (b₂ = 3). A platykurtic distribution (excess kurtosis < 0) has lighter tails than Normal. It often looks flatter near the centre, but it need not; the peak’s shape contributes little to kurtosis (Westfall, 2014).
